comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
CCE94F6651884957A51E6CD8EB2E0EB6.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

6D399F3D0207485A969ADBBBCC3BB9FE.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

6148611CEB8342199AEC71782640C7C9.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

A05F8F03A93F45F2A6CD62E2663E4E4B.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

E688FC70DFE70131534568A86D17958E.description: Analyze and compare two- and three-dimensional shapes, in different sizes and orientations, using informal language to describe their similarities, differences, parts (e.g., number of sides and vertices/"corners") and other attributes (e.g., having sides of equal length).

E688BEC0DFE70131534468A86D17958E.description: Analyze, compare, create, and compose shapes.

E6883CF0DFE70131534268A86D17958E.description: Correctly name shapes regardless of their orientations or overall size.

E687EC30DFE70131534168A86D17958E.description: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes, and describe the relative positions of these objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.

E687A0F0DFE70131534068A86D17958E.description: Identify and describe shapes (squares, circles, triangles, rectangles, hexagons, cubes, cones, cylinders, and spheres).

E68724B0DFE70131533E68A86D17958E.description: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.
comments: Limit category counts to be less than or equal to 10.

E686E050DFE70131533D68A86D17958E.description: Classify objects and count the number of objects in each category.

comments: For example, directly compare the heights of two children and describe one child as taller/shorter.

E6864370DFE70131533B68A86D17958E.description: Describe measurable attributes of objects, such as length or weight. Describe several measurable attributes of a single object.

E68563D0DFE70131533868A86D17958E.description: Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each composition or decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., 18 = 10 + 8); understand that these numbers are composed of ten ones and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

E68522E0DFE70131533768A86D17958E.description: Work with numbers 11—19 to gain foundations for place value.

E684E1F0DFE70131533668A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

E6844F10DFE70131533468A86D17958E.description: For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given number, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record the answer with a drawing or equation.

E683E960DFE70131533368A86D17958E.description: Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., 5 = 2 + 3 and 5 = 4 + 1).

E68383E0DFE70131533268A86D17958E.description: Solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10, e.g., by using objects or drawings to represent the problem.

comments: Drawings need not show details, but should show the mathematics in the problem (This applies wherever drawings are mentioned in the Standards.)
E68334E0DFE70131533168A86D17958E.description: Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.

E682F490DFE70131533068A86D17958E.description: Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.

E6826830DFE70131532E68A86D17958E.description: Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals.

comments: Include groups with up to ten objects.
E68223A0DFE70131532D68A86D17958E.description: Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies.

E681A270DFE70131532B68A86D17958E.description: Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1—20, count out that many objects.

E6816360DFE70131532A68A86D17958E.description: Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.

E68121C0DFE70131532968A86D17958E.description: Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.

E680D5F0DFE70131532868A86D17958E.description: When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object.

E6809420DFE70131532768A86D17958E.description: Understand the relationship between numbers and quantities; connect counting to cardinality.

E68050E0DFE70131532668A86D17958E.description: Count to tell the number of objects.

E6800E50DFE70131532568A86D17958E.description: Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0-20 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).

E67FCC20DFE70131532468A86D17958E.description: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).

E67F8C20DFE70131532368A86D17958E.description: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.

E67F4880DFE70131532268A86D17958E.description: Know number names and the count sequence.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
BB0135C31FC74DDD9E167A4B6587B6BE.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

C37F72950E874CE2AD6914BC59B80D2E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
4ADC95370A4C42BEB4E9E53B65F18F3D.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

F31C7370DFE70131681F68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the structure of texts, including how specific sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text (e.g., a section, chapter, scene, or stanza) relate to each other and the whole.

F31C2730DFE70131681E68A86D17958E.description: Interpret words and phrases as they are used in a text, including determining technical, connotative, and figurative meanings, and analyze how specific word choices shape meaning or tone.

F31B76A0DFE70131681C68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how and why individuals, events, and ideas develop and interact over the course of a text.

F31B20F0DFE70131681B68A86D17958E.description: Determine central ideas or themes of a text and analyze their development; summarize the key supporting details and ideas.

F31ACC40DFE70131681A68A86D17958E.description: Read closely to determine what the text says explicitly and to make logical inferences from it; cite specific textual evidence when writing or speaking to support conclusions drawn from the text.

F31A1A50DFE70131681868A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Reading

document.title: Grade Expectations for Vermont's Framework of Standards and Learning Opportunities

F92066C0DFE701316E7768A86D17958E.description: Analyzing factors involved in the production of a product or service (e.g., developing a business plan for community fundraising).

F9201D30DFE701316E7668A86D17958E.description: Analyzing influences on buying and saving (e.g., media, peers).

F91FD7C0DFE701316E7568A86D17958E.description: Examining the causes and long-term effects of people's needs and/or wants exceeding their available resources, and proposing possible solutions (e.g., examining long term effects of population issues in China and India).

F91F8C60DFE701316E7468A86D17958E.description: Define and apply basic economic concepts such as supply and demand, price, market and/or opportunity cost in an investigation of a regional, national, or international economic question or problem (e.g., In Colombia, what could be an alternative agricultural product to coca?).

F91F3600DFE701316E7368A86D17958E.description: Students make economic decisions as a consumer, producer, saver, investor, and citizen by…

F91EEDE0DFE701316E7268A86D17958E.description: Recognizing that a change in exchange rates changes the relative price of goods and services between two countries (e.g., track the cost in dollars of ordering a Big Mac in Paris over a three week period).

F91E9FD0DFE701316E7168A86D17958E.description: Recognizing that governments around the world create their own currency for use as money (e.g., examining foreign currency for cultural and political symbols).

F91E49B0DFE701316E7068A86D17958E.description: Explaining the relationship between taxation and governmental goods and services in the U.S. and/or world (e.g., how much of the federal budget is devoted to international aid?).

F91DF4D0DFE701316E6F68A86D17958E.description: Evaluating the costs and benefits of government economic programs to both individuals and groups (e.g., debate the pros and cons of welfare programs).

F91DAA00DFE701316E6E68A86D17958E.description: Identifying goods and services provided by local, state, national, and international governmental and/or nongovernmental organizations (e.g., Red Cross, UN peacekeeping efforts, etc.).

F91D5430DFE701316E6D68A86D17958E.description: Students show understanding of the interconnectedness between government and the economy by…

F91D0BB0DFE701316E6C68A86D17958E.description: Drawing conclusions about how choices within an economic system affect the environment in the state, nation, and/or world (e.g., decisions to build "box" stores and new roads).

F91CC120DFE701316E6B68A86D17958E.description: Examining how producers in the U.S. and/or world have used natural, human, and capital resources to produce goods and services, and predicting the long term effects of these uses (e.g., describing how the use of petroleum products will impact the production of hybrid vehicles; examining how the use of human resources in the U.S. has changed over time).

F91C7620DFE701316E6A68A86D17958E.description: Explaining how goods and services around the world create economic interdependence between people in different places (e.g., writing a persuasive essay about the effects of importing oil, exporting labor, etc.).

F91C2800DFE701316E6968A86D17958E.description: Students show an understanding of the interaction/interdependence between humans, the environment, and the economy by…

F91B4FA0DFE701316E6768A86D17958E.description: Identifying and describing examples of tensions between belief systems and government policies and laws, and identifying ways these tensions can be reduced (e.g., Gambling on reservations; neutrality of Switzerland; humanitarian aid).

F91AFB60DFE701316E6668A86D17958E.description: Comparing how different groups gain or have been denied access to various institutions, and describing the impact this has had on these groups in the US and other countries (e.g., Property ownership for voting, ageism, access to education; affirmative action, due process, petition).

F91AB360DFE701316E6568A86D17958E.description: Students examine how access to various institutions affects justice, reward, and power by…

F91A69E0DFE701316E6468A86D17958E.description: Explaining ways in which conflicts can be resolved peacefully (e.g., assimilation /separatism; affirmative action; diplomacy).

F91A1D60DFE701316E6368A86D17958E.description: Explaining conditions, actions, and motivations that contribute to tensions and/or conflict within and among individuals, communities, and nations (e.g., investigating the relationship between poverty and conflict).

F919CFC0DFE701316E6268A86D17958E.description: Analyzing behaviors that foster global cooperation among groups and governments (e.g., lowering trade barriers).

F9197CA0DFE701316E6168A86D17958E.description: Identifying examples of interdependence among states and nations (e.g., transportation systems).

F9193290DFE701316E6068A86D17958E.description: Citing examples, both past and present, of how diversity has led to change. (e.g., immigration of Cubans into Miami).

F918DD10DFE701316E5F68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing differences and similarities among people that arise from factors such as cultural, ethnic, racial, economic, and religious diversity, and describing their costs and benefits.

F9186DC0DFE701316E5E68A86D17958E.description: After examining issues from more than one perspective, defining and defending the rights and needs of others in the community, nation, and world (e.g. AIDS in Africa; One Child Policy in China; nuclear waste disposal).

F91814A0DFE701316E5D68A86D17958E.description: Describing the purposes and functions of governmental and nongovernmental international organizations (e.g., the United Nations, NATO, International Red Cross, Amnesty International).

F917C4C0DFE701316E5C68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing how shared values and beliefs can maintain a subculture (e.g., political parties, religious groups).

F9177C70DFE701316E5B68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing a current or historic issue related to human, rights, and explaining how the values of the time or place influenced the issue (e.g. Kosovo, China, Vietnam).

F9173570DFE701316E5A68A86D17958E.description: Students examine how different societies address issues of human interdependence by…

F916EE40DFE701316E5968A86D17958E.description: Defining criteria for selecting leaders at the school, community, state, national and international levels.

F916A640DFE701316E5868A86D17958E.description: Describing the basic principles of American democracy (e.g., right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness; responsibility for the common good; equality of opportunity and equal protection of the law; freedom of speech and religion).

F9165B20DFE701316E5768A86D17958E.description: Identifying the basic functions, structures and purposes of governments within the United States.

F9160400DFE701316E5668A86D17958E.description: Describing how government decisions impact and/or relate to their lives.

F915BE20DFE701316E5568A86D17958E.description: Identifying key documents on which U.S. laws are based and where to find them (e.g., Declaration of Independence, Bill of Rights, U.S. Constitution).

F9157710DFE701316E5468A86D17958E.description: Describing how rules and laws are created (e.g., participating in a simulation about creating a new law).

F91530C0DFE701316E5368A86D17958E.description: Students show understanding of various forms of government by…

F914E850DFE701316E5268A86D17958E.description: Establishing rules and/or policies for a group, school, or community, and defending them (e.g., dress code policies, establishing a skate board park).

F9149780DFE701316E5168A86D17958E.description: Demonstrating how identity stems from beliefs in and allegiance to shared political values and principles, and how these are similar and different to other peoples (e.g. Northern Ireland/Republic; socialism; capitalism).

F91448B0DFE701316E5068A86D17958E.description: Illustrating how individuals and groups have brought about change locally, nationally, or internationally (e.g., interview someone involved in civil union legislation).

F913FAC0DFE701316E4F68A86D17958E.description: Giving examples of ways in which political parties, campaigns, and elections provide opportunities for citizens to participate in the political process.

F913A480DFE701316E4E68A86D17958E.description: Explaining and critically evaluating views that are not one's own.

F9135640DFE701316E4D68A86D17958E.description: Explaining and defending their own point of view on issues that affect themselves and society, using information gained from reputable sources (e.g. communism vs. democracy; war vs. economic sanctions).

F91300A0DFE701316E4C68A86D17958E.description: Identifying problems, proposing solutions, and considering the effects of a course of action in the local community, state, nation, or world.

F912A2D0DFE701316E4B68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrating positive interaction with group members (e.g., working with a group to design a lesson teaching younger students about rights and responsibilities).

F9125DC0DFE701316E4A68A86D17958E.description: Giving examples of ways people act as members of a global community (e.g., collecting used textbooks for countries in need).

F9121720DFE701316E4968A86D17958E.description: Identifying the various ways people become citizens of the U.S. (e.g., birth, naturalization).

F911D0A0DFE701316E4868A86D17958E.description: Comparing the rights and responsibilities of citizenship in another country to those of the U.S (e.g., after reading accounts of elections in news articles, compare voting rights)

F910E520DFE701316E4568A86D17958E.description: Identifying ways in which culture in the United States and the world has changed and may change in the future (e.g., the spread of Islam).

F9109D90DFE701316E4468A86D17958E.description: Analyzing how location and spatial patterns influence the spread of cultural traits (e.g., comparing clothing, food, religion/values, government, and art across four ancient cultures in relation to location).

F91056E0DFE701316E4368A86D17958E.description: Describing the contributions of various cultural groups to the world, both past and present.

F9101040DFE701316E4268A86D17958E.description: Identifying and comparing expressions of culture in Vermont, the U.S., and the world through analysis of various modes of expression such as poems, songs, dances, stories, paintings, and photographs (e.g., identifying how the Japanese art of Gyotaku [fish printing] reflects history and culture).

F90FC750DFE701316E4168A86D17958E.description: Students analyze how and why cultures continue and change over time by…

F90F7F50DFE701316E4068A86D17958E.description: Using information to make predictions about future migration.

F90F2180DFE701316E3F68A86D17958E.description: Recognizing patterns of voluntary and involuntary migration in the U.S. and world.

F90ECA80DFE701316E3E68A86D17958E.description: Examining multiple factors in the interaction of humans and the environment (e.g., population size, farmland, and food production).

F90E7430DFE701316E3D68A86D17958E.description: Evaluating different viewpoints regarding resource use in the U.S. and world (e.g., debating drilling for oil in a national wildlife refuge).

F90E2D60DFE701316E3C68A86D17958E.description: Generating information related to the impact of human activities on the physical environment (for example, through field studies, mapping, interviewing, and using scientific instruments) in order to draw conclusions and recommend actions (e.g., damming the Yangtze River).

F90DE610DFE701316E3B68A86D17958E.description: Describing how human activity and technology have changed the environment in the U.S. and world for specific purposes (e.g., development of urban environments, genetic modification of crops, flood control, reforestation).

F90D9930DFE701316E3A68A86D17958E.description: Students show understanding of human interaction with the environment over time by…

F90D3F30DFE701316E3968A86D17958E.description: Comparing and contrasting spatial patterns or landforms using geographic resources (e.g., comparing water usage between nations).

F90CCC90DFE701316E3868A86D17958E.description: Using grid systems to locate places on maps and globes (e.g., longitude and latitude).

F90C80B0DFE701316E3768A86D17958E.description: Identifying and using basic elements of a variety of maps.

F90C38C0DFE701316E3668A86D17958E.description: Interpreting a variety of effective representations of the earth such as maps, globes, and photographs and project future changes (e.g., physical, political, topographic, computer generated, and special purpose maps).

F90BF0A0DFE701316E3568A86D17958E.description: Using absolute and relative location to identifying major mountain ranges, major rivers, and major climate and vegetation zones and the effects of these on settlement patterns (e.g., Appalachian Mountain's effect on westward movement; overgrazing; Palestinian/Israeli conflict).

F90B9B50DFE701316E3468A86D17958E.description: Locating and using absolute and relative location, and explaining why selected cities are of historical and current importance (e.g., Palestine; Moscow).

F90B48A0DFE701316E3368A86D17958E.description: Locating the physical, political, and cultural regions of the United States and the world (e.g., Sub-Sahara, Middle East, Eurasia).

F90B02B0DFE701316E3268A86D17958E.description: Observing, comparing, and analyzing patterns of national, and global land use (e.g., agriculture, forestry, industry) to understand why particular locations are used for certain human activities.

F90AB7A0DFE701316E3168A86D17958E.description: Identifying characteristics of states, countries, and continents using resources such as landmarks, models, different kinds of maps, photographs, atlases, internet, video, reference materials, GIS and mental mapping.

F90A6AF0DFE701316E3068A86D17958E.description: Students interpret geography and solve geographic problems by…

F9099870DFE701316E2E68A86D17958E.description: Identifying why certain events are considered pivotal and how they cause us to reorder time (e.g., the explosion of the atom bomb and the beginning of the nuclear age; September 11, 2001).

F90935B0DFE701316E2D68A86D17958E.description: Explaining transitions between eras that occurred over time (e.g. independence of African nations) as well as those that occurred as a result of a pivotal event (e.g., the invention of the automobile and the light bulb).

F908F2A0DFE701316E2C68A86D17958E.description: Identifying important events in the United States and/or world, and describing multiple causes and effects of those events.

F908ADE0DFE701316E2B68A86D17958E.description: Making predictions and/or decisions based on an understanding of the past and the present (e.g., after analyzing past events, determining what steps can impact the future).

F9086860DFE701316E2A68A86D17958E.description: Understanding a variety of calendars (e.g., Islamic, Jewish, Chinese) and reasons for their organizational structures (e.g., political, historic, religious).

F9081B00DFE701316E2968A86D17958E.description: Measuring and calculating calendar time by days, weeks, months, years, decades, centuries, and millennia (e.g., How long ago did people first come to North America?).

F907C440DFE701316E2868A86D17958E.description: Interpreting data presented in time lines.

F9076670DFE701316E2768A86D17958E.description: Constructing time lines of significant historical developments in the nation and world, designating appropriate equidistant intervals of time and recording events according to the order in which they occurred.

F906F500DFE701316E2668A86D17958E.description: Identifying the beginning, middle, and end of an historical narrative or story.

F906A810DFE701316E2568A86D17958E.description: Students show understanding of past, present and future time by…

F9065DF0DFE701316E2468A86D17958E.description: Identifying how technology can lead to a different interpretation of history (e.g., DNA evidence, forensic analysis of a battle site).

F9060760DFE701316E2368A86D17958E.description: Evaluating attitudes, values, and behaviors of people in different historical contexts (e.g., examining how religious values have influenced historic events).

F905BE90DFE701316E2268A86D17958E.description: Evaluating the credibility of differing accounts of the same event(s) (e.g., account of the Revolutionary War from a colonist's perspective vs. British perspective; the bombing of Hiroshima from the perspective of a Japanese citizen vs. an American soldier).

F9052F00DFE701316E2068A86D17958E.description: Identifying different types of primary and secondary sources (for example, visual, literary, and musical sources), and evaluating the possible biases expressed in them (e.g., analyzing Paul Revere's engraving of the Boston Massacre).

F904D890DFE701316E1F68A86D17958E.description: Students show understanding of how humans interpret history by…

F9046350DFE701316E1E68A86D17958E.description: Investigating and evaluating how events, people, and ideas (democracy, for example) have shaped the United States and the world, and hypothesizing how different influences could have led to different consequences (e.g., How did the ideals of Greek democracy impact the world? How has European colonialism influenced race relations in Africa?).

F9040490DFE701316E1D68A86D17958E.description: Describing ways that life in the United States and/or the world has both changed and stayed the same over time, and explaining why these changes have occurred (e.g., In what ways would the life of a teenager during the American Revolution be different from the life of a teenager today? What factors have contributed to these differences?).

F903C010DFE701316E1C68A86D17958E.description: Explaining differences between historic and present day objects in the United States and/or the world, and evaluating how the use of the object and the object itself changed over time (e.g., comparing modes of transportation used in past and present exploration in order to evaluate impact and the effects of those changes).

F9037BD0DFE701316E1B68A86D17958E.description: Students connect the past with the present by…

F902F2C0DFE701316E1968A86D17958E.description:
• Developing and giving oral, written, or visual presentations for various audiences.
  • Soliciting and responding to feedback.
  • Pointing out possibilities for continued or further research.

F9024F10DFE701316E1768A86D17958E.description:
• Formulating recommendations and/or making decisions based on evidence.
  • Using their research results to support or refute the original research statement.
  • Proposing solutions to problems based on their findings, and asking additional questions.
  • Identifying problems or flaws with the research plan and suggesting improvements (e.g., identifying additional types of information that could strengthen an investigation).
  • Proposing further investigations.

F901FFF0DFE701316E1668A86D17958E.description: Students make connections to research by…

F901B120DFE701316E1568A86D17958E.description:
• Organizing and display information in a manner appropriate to the research statement through tables graphs, maps, dioramas, charts, narratives, posters timelines, models, simulations, and/or dramatizations.
  • Determining the validity and reliability of the document or information.
  • Choosing and using appropriate methods for interpreting information, such as comparing and contrasting, summarizing, illustrating, generalizing, sequencing, synthesizing, analyzing, and/or justifying (e.g., analyzing information to determine why two historical accounts of the same event might differ.)
  • Revising explanations as necessary based on personal reflection, peer critique, expert opinion, etc.

F90164E0DFE701316E1468A86D17958E.description: Students develop reasonable explanations that support the research statement by…

F9011C30DFE701316E1368A86D17958E.description:
• Referring to and following a detailed plan for an inquiry.
  • Locating relevant materials such as print, electronic, and human resources.
  • Applying criteria from the plan to analyze the quality and
  • quantity of information gathered (e.g., judging the accuracy of different accounts of the same event).
  • Describing evidence and recording observations using notecards, videotape, tape recorders, journals, or databases.
  • Revising the research plan and locating additional materials and/or information, as needed.
  • Citing sources.

F9004000DFE701316E1068A86D17958E.description: Determining possible ways to present data (e.g., PowerPoint, hypercard, report, graph, etc.).

F8FFFCE0DFE701316E0F68A86D17958E.description: Identifying tools and procedures needed for collecting, managing, and examining information, including a plan for citing sources (e.g., establishing a time line or schedule for research, identifying places to find possible sources).

F8FFB9A0DFE701316E0E68A86D17958E.description: Identifying the quality and quantity of information needed, including primary and secondary sources.

F8FEE570DFE701316E0B68A86D17958E.description: Predicting results, proposing a choice about a possible action, or exploring relationships between facts and/or concepts.

F8FE94D0DFE701316E0A68A86D17958E.description: Students develop a hypothesis, thesis, or research statement by…

F8FDF100DFE701316E0868A86D17958E.description: Asking focusing and probing questions that will lead to independent research and incorporate concepts of personal, community, or global relevance (e.g., What are the causes of low voter turnout? What are the most effective ways to improve voter participation?).

document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

E82E8870DFE70131556968A86D17958E.description: (+) Work with 2 × 2 matrices as transformations of the plane, and interpret the absolute value of the determinant in terms of area.

E82E3040DFE70131556868A86D17958E.description: (+) Multiply a vector (regarded as a matrix with one column) by a matrix of suitable dimensions to produce another vector. Work with matrices as transformations of vectors.

E82DD4E0DFE70131556768A86D17958E.description: (+) Understand that the zero and identity matrices play a role in matrix addition and multiplication similar to the role of 0 and 1 in the real numbers. The determinant of a square matrix is nonzero if and only if the matrix has a multiplicative inverse.

E8302A40DFE70131556D68A86D17958E.description: (+) Understand that, unlike multiplication of numbers, matrix multiplication for square matrices is not a commutative operation, but still satisfies the associative and distributive properties.

E82FC330DFE70131556C68A86D17958E.description: (+) Add, subtract, and multiply matrices of appropriate dimensions.

E82F5720DFE70131556B68A86D17958E.description: (+) Multiply matrices by scalars to produce new matrices, e.g., as when all of the payoffs in a game are doubled.

E82EF620DFE70131556A68A86D17958E.description: (+) Use matrices to represent and manipulate data, e.g., to represent payoffs or incidence relationships in a network.

E82D8080DFE70131556668A86D17958E.description: Perform operations on matrices and use matrices in applications.

E82D29C0DFE70131556568A86D17958E.description: Compute the magnitude of a scalar multiple cv using ||cv|| = |c|v. Compute the direction of cv knowing that when |c|v ? 0, the direction of cv is either along v (for c > 0) or against v (for c < 0).

E82CD2E0DFE70131556468A86D17958E.description: Represent scalar multiplication graphically by scaling vectors and possibly reversing their direction; perform scalar multiplication component-wise, e.g., as c(v<sub>x</sub>, v<sub>y</sub>) = (cv<sub>x</sub>, cv<sub>y</sub>).

E82C7820DFE70131556368A86D17958E.description: (+) Multiply a vector by a scalar.

E82C10D0DFE70131556268A86D17958E.description: Understand vector subtraction v - w as v + (-w), where -w is the additive inverse of w, with the same magnitude as w and pointing in the opposite direction. Represent vector subtraction graphically by connecting the tips in the appropriate order, and perform vector subtraction component-wise.

E82BB3E0DFE70131556168A86D17958E.description: Given two vectors in magnitude and direction form, determine the magnitude and direction of their sum.

E82B5070DFE70131556068A86D17958E.description: Add vectors end-to-end, component-wise, and by the parallelogram rule. Understand that the magnitude of a sum of two vectors is typically not the sum of the magnitudes.

E82A2030DFE70131555D68A86D17958E.description: (+) Solve problems involving velocity and other quantities that can be represented by vectors.

E829C980DFE70131555C68A86D17958E.description: (+) Find the components of a vector by subtracting the coordinates of an initial point from the coordinates of a terminal point.

E82961A0DFE70131555B68A86D17958E.description: (+) Recognize vector quantities as having both magnitude and direction. Represent vector quantities by directed line segments, and use appropriate symbols for vectors and their magnitudes (e.g., v, |v|, ||v||, v).

E828EED0DFE70131555A68A86D17958E.description: Represent and model with vector quantities.

E8283380DFE70131555868A86D17958E.description: (+) Know the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra; show that it is true for quadratic polynomials.

E827DC50DFE70131555768A86D17958E.description: (+) Extend polynomial identities to the complex numbers.
comments: For example, rewrite x² + 4 as (x + 2i)(x - 2i).

E82784E0DFE70131555668A86D17958E.description: Solve quadratic equations with real coefficients that have complex solutions.

E8272AA0DFE70131555568A86D17958E.description: Use complex numbers in polynomial identities and equations.

E826CCF0DFE70131555468A86D17958E.description: (+) Calculate the distance between numbers in the complex plane as the modulus of the difference, and the midpoint of a segment as the average of the numbers at its endpoints.

comments: For example, (-1 + √3 i)³ = 8 because (-1 + √3 i) has modulus 2 and argument 120°.
E8265BC0DFE70131555368A86D17958E.description: (+) Represent addition, subtraction, multiplication, and conjugation of complex numbers geometrically on the complex plane; use properties of this representation for computation.

E825FB70DFE70131555268A86D17958E.description: (+) Represent complex numbers on the complex plane in rectangular and polar form (including real and imaginary numbers), and explain why the rectangular and polar forms of a given complex number represent the same number.

E82596B0DFE70131555168A86D17958E.description: Represent complex numbers and their operations on the complex plane.

E82531E0DFE70131555068A86D17958E.description: (+) Find the conjugate of a complex number; use conjugates to find moduli and quotients of complex numbers.

E824D620DFE70131554F68A86D17958E.description: Use the relation i² = -1 and the commutative, associative, and distributive properties to add, subtract, and multiply complex numbers.

E8247730DFE70131554E68A86D17958E.description: Know there is a complex number i such that i² = -1, and every complex number has the form a + bi with a and b real.

E8241D40DFE70131554D68A86D17958E.description: Perform arithmetic operations with complex numbers.

E8235110DFE70131554B68A86D17958E.description: Choose a level of accuracy appropriate to limitations on measurement when reporting quantities.

E822F4F0DFE70131554A68A86D17958E.description: Define appropriate quantities for the purpose of descriptive modeling.

E82294B0DFE70131554968A86D17958E.description: Use units as a way to understand problems and to guide the solution of multi-step problems; choose and interpret units consistently in formulas; choose and interpret the scale and the origin in graphs and data displays.

E8223B30DFE70131554868A86D17958E.description: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems.

comments: Modeling is best interpreted not as a collection of isolated topics but in relation to other standards. Making mathematical models is a Standard for Mathematical Practice, and specific modeling standards appear throughout the high school standards indicated by a star symbol (★). The star symbol sometimes appears on the heading for a group of standards; in that case, it should be understood to apply to all standards in that group.

E82184B0DFE70131554668A86D17958E.description: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational; that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational; and that the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is irrational.

E8212620DFE70131554568A86D17958E.description: Use properties of rational and irrational numbers.

E820B6E0DFE70131554468A86D17958E.description: Rewrite expressions involving radicals and rational exponents using the properties of exponents.

E8204C60DFE70131554368A86D17958E.description: Explain how the definition of the meaning of rational exponents follows from extending the properties of integer exponents to those values, allowing for a notation for radicals in terms of rational exponents.
comments: For example, we define 5<sup>1/3</sup> to be the cube root of 5 because we want (5<sup>1/3</sup>)³ = 5(<sup>1/3</sup>)³ to hold, so (5<sup>1/3</sup>)³ must equal 5.

E81FEB60DFE70131554268A86D17958E.description: Extend the properties of exponents to rational exponents.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
413AD53AC0B5466E96828ED96480E7EC.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

96D843B5293B4BE58932761CDDB918FB.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

56A5140858D340E6818D39AF7A878E40.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

C55170F81178402DAC49BDE31EFC8F1C.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

E75B5900DFE70131542B68A86D17958E.description: Compare two decimals to hundredths by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two decimals refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual model.

E75B1320DFE70131542A68A86D17958E.description: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100.
comments: For example, rewrite 0.62 as 62/100; describe a length as 0.62 meters; locate 0.62 on a number line diagram.

E75ACDC0DFE70131542968A86D17958E.description: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100, and use this technique to add two fractions with respective denominators 10 and 100.
comments: Students who can generate equivalent fractions can develop strategies for adding fractions with unlike denominators in general. But addition and subtraction with unlike denominators in general is not a requirement at this grade.
For example, express 3/10 as 30/100, and add 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100.

E75A89D0DFE70131542868A86D17958E.description: Understand decimal notation for fractions, and compare decimal fractions.

comments: For example, if each person at a party will eat 3/8 of a pound of roast beef, and there will be 5 people at the party, how many pounds of roast beef will be needed? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
E75A3D30DFE70131542768A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

E759EA00DFE70131542668A86D17958E.description: Understand a multiple of a/b as a multiple of 1/b, and use this understanding to multiply a fraction by a whole number.
comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to express 3 × (2/5) as 6 × (1/5), recognizing this product as 6/5. (In general, n × (a/b) = (n × a)/b.)

E759A1D0DFE70131542568A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction a/b as a multiple of 1/b.
comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to represent 5/4 as the product 5 × (1/4), recording the conclusion by the equation 5/4 = 5 × (1/4).

E7595F90DFE70131542468A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction by a whole number.

E7591C90DFE70131542368A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and having like denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

E758D830DFE70131542268A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

E7588CB0DFE70131542168A86D17958E.description: Decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way, recording each decomposition by an equation. Justify decompositions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

E7583F70DFE70131542068A86D17958E.description: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole.

E757FBF0DFE70131541F68A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction a/b with a > 1 as a sum of fractions 1/b.

E757B4C0DFE70131541E68A86D17958E.description: Build fractions from unit fractions by applying and extending previous understandings of operations on whole numbers.

E7576300DFE70131541D68A86D17958E.description: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators, e.g., by creating common denominators or numerators, or by comparing to a benchmark fraction such as 1/2. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

E7571030DFE70131541C68A86D17958E.description: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to a fraction (n × a)/(n × b) by using visual fraction models, with attention to how the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Use this principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.

E756B920DFE70131541B68A86D17958E.description: Extend understanding of fraction equivalence and ordering.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100

E7561C50DFE70131541968A86D17958E.description: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure as a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into matching parts. Identify line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.

E755C2B0DFE70131541868A86D17958E.description: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or the presence or absence of angles of a specified size. Recognize right triangles as a category, and identify right triangles.

E7557D70DFE70131541768A86D17958E.description: Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures.

E7553980DFE70131541668A86D17958E.description: Draw and identify lines and angles, and classify shapes by properties of their lines and angles.

E754A900DFE70131541468A86D17958E.description: Recognize angle measure as additive. When an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts, the angle measure of the whole is the sum of the angle measures of the parts. Solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram in real world and mathematical problems, e.g., by using an equation with a symbol for the unknown angle measure.

E75466E0DFE70131541368A86D17958E.description: Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor. Sketch angles of specified measure.

E7542260DFE70131541268A86D17958E.description: An angle that turns through n one-degree angles is said to have an angle measure of n degrees.

E753DFD0DFE70131541168A86D17958E.description: An angle is measured with reference to a circle with its center at the common endpoint of the rays, by considering the fraction of the circular arc between the points where the two rays intersect the circle. An angle that turns through 1/360 of a circle is called a "one-degree angle," and can be used to measure angles.

E7539BB0DFE70131541068A86D17958E.description: Recognize angles as geometric shapes that are formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint, and understand concepts of angle measurement:

E75353C0DFE70131540F68A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of angle and measure angles.

comments: For example, from a line plot find and interpret the difference in length between the longest and shortest specimens in an insect collection.
E751B9F0DFE70131540A68A86D17958E.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.

comments: For example, find the width of a rectangular room given the area of the flooring and the length, by viewing the area formula as a multiplication equation with an unknown factor.
E7530460DFE70131540E68A86D17958E.description: Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real world and mathematical problems.

E752BEE0DFE70131540D68A86D17958E.description: Use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Represent measurement quantities using diagrams such as number line diagrams that feature a measurement scale.

comments: For example, know that 1 ft is 12 times as long as 1 in. Express the length of a 4 ft snake as 48 in. Generate a conversion table for feet and inches listing the number pairs (1, 12), (2, 24), (3, 36), …
E7526560DFE70131540C68A86D17958E.description: Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system of units including km, m, cm; kg, g; lb, oz.; l, ml; hr, min, sec. Within a single system of measurement, express measurements in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Record measurement equivalents in a two column table.

E7521380DFE70131540B68A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving measurement and conversion of measurements from a larger unit to a smaller unit.

E74FA790DFE70131540368A86D17958E.description: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

E74F5A40DFE70131540268A86D17958E.description: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

E74F1270DFE70131540168A86D17958E.description: Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

E74ECCC0DFE70131540068A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.

E750D840DFE70131540768A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.

E7508CE0DFE70131540668A86D17958E.description: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form. Compare two multi-digit numbers based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

E7503DC0DFE70131540568A86D17958E.description: Recognize that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right.
comments: For example, recognize that 700 ÷ 70 = 10 by applying concepts of place value and division.

E74FF520DFE70131540468A86D17958E.description: Generalize place value understanding for multi-digit whole numbers.

E74E85A0DFE7013153FF68A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

E74E3970DFE7013153FE68A86D17958E.description: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself.
comments: For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.

E74D9C30DFE7013153FC68A86D17958E.description: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1—100. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1—100 is a multiple of a given one-digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1—100 is prime or composite.

E74D5070DFE7013153FB68A86D17958E.description: Gain familiarity with factors and multiples.

E74CFFB0DFE7013153FA68A86D17958E.description: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.

E74CAFD0DFE7013153F968A86D17958E.description: Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.

E74C6340DFE7013153F868A86D17958E.description: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, e.g., interpret 35 = 5 × 7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.

E74C1BD0DFE7013153F768A86D17958E.description: Use the four operations with whole numbers to solve problems.

document.title: Common Core Standards for English Language Arts and Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science and Technical Subjects

F1837EA0DFE70131650968A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases, including those that signal precise actions, emotions, or states of being (e.g., quizzed, whined, stammered) and that are basic to a particular topic (e.g., wildlife, conservation, and endangered when discussing animal preservation).

F1831700DFE70131650868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of words by relating them to their opposites (antonyms) and to words with similar but not identical meanings (synonyms).

F182CB80DFE70131650768A86D17958E.description: Recognize and explain the meaning of common idioms, adages, and proverbs.

F1828090DFE70131650668A86D17958E.description: Explain the meaning of simple similes and metaphors (e.g., as pretty as a picture) in context.

F18234B0DFE70131650568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

F181E420DFE70131650468A86D17958E.description: Consult reference materials (e.g., dictionaries, glossaries, thesauruses), both print and digital, to find the pronunciation and determine or clarify the precise meaning of key words and phrases.

F1819210DFE70131650368A86D17958E.description: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek and Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word (e.g., telegraph, photograph, autograph).

F18146C0DFE70131650268A86D17958E.description: Use context (e.g., definitions, examples, or restatements in text) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

F180FCC0DFE70131650168A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 4 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.

F1805620DFE7013164FF68A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between contexts that call for formal English (e.g., presenting ideas) and situations where informal discourse is appropriate (e.g., small-group discussion).

F17F7DE0DFE7013164FD68A86D17958E.description: Choose words and phrases to convey ideas precisely.

F17F30A0DFE7013164FC68A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.

F17E9720DFE7013164FA68A86D17958E.description: Spell grade-appropriate words correctly, consulting references as needed.

F17E4B20DFE7013164F968A86D17958E.description: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction in a compound sentence.

F17DF2C0DFE7013164F868A86D17958E.description: Use commas and quotation marks to mark direct speech and quotations from a text.

F17D5870DFE7013164F668A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

F17D0BA0DFE7013164F568A86D17958E.description: Correctly use frequently confused words (e.g., to, too, two; there, their).
